title: A solver-by-objective grid asks: does the answer depend on the optimizer, the objective, or both?
summary: Nine small landscapes in a three-by-three grid: three optimizers across the columns, three objectives down the rows, each with the start, the true optimum, the search path and two printed numbers. The grid is read by comparing the distance to the true optimum, not the objective value, because the objective is different in every row.

media.alt: A three by three grid of contour panels. Columns: gradient descent, GA, CMA-ES. Rows: classical WMRE, fixed p = 0.05, annealed p from 4 to 0.05. Each panel has a black start, a green star for the true optimum, a pink search path and two printed numbers, obj and dist. The first row shows smooth bowls with dist 0.002; in the lower rows several panels show dist about 0.6 and others about 0.004.

source.caption: Gradient descent, GA and CMA-ES on the toy landscape: WMRE, fixed p and annealed p

read_the_figure.question: For each combination of optimizer and objective, did the search end at the true optimum?
read_the_figure.axes: Each panel has z1 on x and z2 on y, both from minus 1 to 1, with the objective as filled contours. Columns: gradient descent, genetic algorithm (GA), CMA-ES. Rows: the classical WMRE, a fixed exponent p = 0.05, and an annealed exponent from 4 to 0.05. Black dot: start. Pink line: search path. Green star: true optimum. Blue star: result of a final local refinement stage (L-BFGS-B polish). Grey dots: local minima. Dashed contours: pre-anneal surface. The two numbers in each panel are the final objective (obj) and the distance from the final point to the true optimum (dist).
look_at: Read dist first. It is the same quantity in all nine panels (distance in the standardized parameter plane to the green star), so it is the one number that can be compared across rows.
Do not compare obj down a column: the objective is different in each row (the first row has values like 18, the others values near 0.1 to 0.3).
Row 1 (classical): every solver ends essentially at the star, because the surface is a single bowl.
Rows 2 and 3: panels with a small dist found the optimum; panels with a dist of about 0.6 stopped in a local minimum, and the blue star shows where the polish left them.

Compare the same solver in rows 2 and 3. A solver whose panel is unchanged between the rows (the gradient-descent column here) is insensitive to the annealing; a solver whose panel improves (the CMA-ES column here) benefits from it.
read_the_figure.proves: On this one toy surface and one starting point, which optimizer and objective combinations reach the true optimum. It does not rank the methods in general: nine runs, one start, one surface.
if_wrong: A panel with a low obj but a large dist: a local minimum, a good-looking but wrong answer.

Identical numbers in two panels (as in the two gradient-descent panels with a different objective): a deterministic method stuck on the same valley, or a surface in which the annealing makes no difference to that solver's path.
A tiny dist where the start is already close: no information about the method.
A pink path that ends somewhere but a blue star elsewhere: the refinement stage moved the result; say which of the two the printed numbers refer to.
must_check: dist is defined and measured in one coordinate system for all panels.
The objective values in different rows are not compared.
The number of runs per panel and whether the stochastic solvers were seeded.
All three rows share the same start point.
The legend explains every symbol, including the refinement stage.

terms.meaning: An iterative method that steps against the local slope. Deterministic: the same start gives the same path.
A population method that keeps a set of candidate points and repeatedly selects, recombines and mutates them. Needs no gradient and is stochastic.
Covariance matrix adaptation evolution strategy: a stochastic population method that adapts a Gaussian search distribution to the surface. Gradient-free.
The Euclidean distance between the final point and the true optimum in the parameter plane. Defined because the optimum is known here.
A final short gradient-based stage that tightens the result of the main search. It improves the position within its own valley; it cannot move the point to another valley.
For positive numbers s_1..s_D, the generalized mean of exponent p. It is an ordinary average when p = 1, a geometric mean as p goes to 0, and it approaches the largest value as p grows.

remember: Compare dist, not obj, across rows.
A refinement stage tightens a result inside its valley; it does not change the valley.
A deterministic solver gives the same answer from the same start; a stochastic one needs replicates.
A single start and a single surface is a demonstration, not a ranking.
If two objectives give the same optimum on a smooth surface, the difference between them only shows on a hard one.

understand.title: Why three solvers
understand.text: The three solvers explore differently: gradient descent follows the local slope, GA and CMA-ES sample populations. A surface with many valleys separates them by how far they look before committing.

understand.title: Why the grid is read by rows and columns
understand.text: Reading across a row holds the objective fixed and varies the solver; reading down a column holds the solver fixed and varies the objective. Whatever differs along one direction but not the other is attributable to that factor.

understand.title: Read the printed numbers literally
understand.text: On this figure the final panels of the grid show that the same solver can give an identical answer under two objectives while another solver changes. Those are the numbers printed in the panels, for this one toy surface.

steps.title: Distance in the parameter plane
steps.note: The Euclidean distance. A panel whose printed dist is about 0.6 ended roughly 0.6 away from the star in standardized coordinates, which is a large fraction of the half-width of the plane (1).

steps.title: Deterministic descent has no randomness to average
steps.note: From a fixed start this sequence is fixed. Two different objectives with the same local valley near the start can then give the very same path, as the two gradient-descent panels do here.

steps.title: Stochastic solvers: results are random variables
steps.note: A stochastic panel is one draw. Its spread over n seeds, sigma, and the standard error sigma over the square root of n say how far one draw can be trusted.

steps.title: Probability of success from repeated runs
steps.note: If k of n seeded runs end within a tolerance of the optimum, this is the estimated success rate and its approximate standard error. Nine panels are not enough to estimate it.

steps.title: Why a polish cannot cross a valley
steps.tex: f(x_{k+1})\le f(x_k)\ \text{(monotone descent)}\ \Rightarrow\ \text{iterates stay in the basin of the starting valley}
steps.note: For a method that only goes downhill, the limit point is the minimum of the basin it started in, so a final local refinement tightens the result but cannot rescue a wrong valley.

worked.title: Check a printed distance from the picture
worked.problem: In the fixed-exponent gradient-descent panel the blue star is at about (0, -0.35) and the green star at about (0.63, -0.35), read by eye. Does that agree with the printed dist = 0.629?

solution.text: Difference in z1 and in z2.

worked.answer: 0.63, which matches the printed 0.629. The numbers in the panel are consistent with the picture; this checks that dist is a distance to the green star.

analyze.q: Two panels in different rows have the same distance but very different obj. What does that tell you?
analyze.hint: The objective scale is a property of the row.

analyze.q: The gradient-descent result is identical under the fixed and the annealed objectives. Give two explanations.
analyze.hint: Same valley near the start; the annealed phase did not change the local slope that determines the first steps.

analyze.q: CMA-ES ends away from the star under one objective and at it under another. Does one panel prove the second objective is better?

evaluate.q: Can the grid support the statement that annealing helps in general?
evaluate.hint: Count solvers, starts, surfaces and seeds.

evaluate.q: Which additional experiment would turn the grid into evidence?
evaluate.hint: Many starts and seeds; report success fractions with their standard errors.

create: Replace each panel by a success-rate bar over 50 random starts, with a standard-error whisker, and keep one example path as an inset.
Add a fourth row for a still smaller fixed exponent and predict what the panels will show.

checks.q: Which printed number can be compared across rows?
checks.hint: One of the two is defined the same way everywhere.
checks.answer: dist, the distance to the true optimum. obj is a different quantity in each row.

checks.q: A result is at (0.1, -0.3) and the optimum at (0.6, -0.3). What is dist?
A panel shows a small obj but a large dist. Interpretation?
checks.answer: A local minimum: a good-looking objective at the wrong place.

checks.q: Seven of ten seeded runs reach the optimum. How certain is the success rate?
checks.hint: Use the standard error of a proportion.
checks.answer: P = 0.7 with a standard error of about 0.14, so the real rate could plausibly be anywhere from about 0.4 to 1.

checks.q: How would you separate the effect of the objective from the effect of the solver?
checks.answer: Run every solver on every objective from the same set of starts (a full factorial), then compare success rates along rows and columns.
